title: The tenant boundary is a query, not a checkbox
dek: Multi-tenant authorization fails in the same place again and again: the code knows who the user is, but not which rows that user is allowed to touch. The durable fix is not a controller check. It is a data-layer constraint.
html:
A multi-tenant application can pass every authentication test and still leak every customer’s data. The login is correct. The session is valid. The role check runs. The bug is one layer lower: the object being requested is fetched by an identifier the user controls, from a dataset that is not scoped to their tenant.

This is usually described as BOLA — broken object-level authorization — or IDOR. The labels are useful, but they can make the problem sound like a missing if statement. It is more useful to think of it as a missing invariant: every object access must be evaluated inside a tenant scope.

Authentication answers the wrong question

Authentication asks: who is this? The tenant boundary asks a second question: is this row inside the caller’s tenant? A request can satisfy the first and fail the second. When an endpoint fetches a record globally and only checks that the caller is logged in, the identifier in the URL becomes an authorization decision made by the client.

If the database query does not know about the tenant, the controller is already too late.

The failure pattern, in four shapes

The same root cause appears in predictable places. When I test a multi-tenant product, I look for all four:

  • Direct object access. A detail endpoint fetches by a public or sequential identifier and checks only is_authenticated.
  • Collection leakage. A list, search, dashboard, or export endpoint queries a global table and filters in the serializer or template.
  • Nested objects. A case is scoped correctly, but its comments, files, staff members, or audit entries are fetched through a separate unscoped query.
  • Write-path gaps. Reads are scoped, but a PATCH, assignment, comment, or bulk action resolves the object through a different code path.

The dangerous ones are rarely the obvious “get user by id” route. They are the background job, the CSV export, the notification preview, the GraphQL node resolver, and the admin convenience endpoint that was added after the authorization review.

A test matrix that finds the gap

A two-tenant test pair is the most efficient tool I know for this class of bug. Create Tenant A and Tenant B, each with a user at the same role, and one object in each tenant. Then test every action as A against B’s object. Repeat with different roles, because the bug may exist only for a lower-privileged user.

ActorObjectActionExpected
Tenant A userTenant B recordRead404 or 403
Tenant A userTenant B recordUpdate404 or 403
Tenant A userTenant B collectionList / exportOnly own rows
Tenant A adminTenant B recordAssign / delete404 or 403
AnonymousAny recordRead401

Then extend the matrix to the less obvious surfaces: search, pagination, bulk update, file download, comment threads, audit logs, notifications, GraphQL nodes, and any endpoint that accepts an array of identifiers. A single missed route is enough.

Why controller checks drift

A typical first fix looks like this: fetch the object, compare its organization to the current user, and return an error if they differ. It works for the route where the bug was found. It does not create an invariant. New routes, new serializers, new background jobs, and refactors can bypass the check without anyone noticing.

The better pattern is to make the scoped queryset the only way to reach the model in request-handling code, then enforce ownership at retrieval time. The code should look boring: 

# The tenant comes from the authenticated session, never from a header or body.
class CaseQuerySet(models.QuerySet):
    def for_tenant(self, tenant):
        return self.filter(organization=tenant)
def get_case(request, public_id):
    return get_object_or_404(
        Case.objects.for_tenant(request.tenant),
        public_id=public_id,
    )

This does two things at once. It makes the common path safe by default, and it makes the unsafe path visible in review: a query without for_tenant() is now an exception that needs a reason.

Design rule

Never derive the tenant from client-controlled input. Take it from the authenticated session or a trusted server-side mapping. A tenant header is an assertion, not an identity.

Make the fix testable

A boundary that is not tested will drift. Add a small regression suite that creates two tenants, signs in as each, and asserts that cross-tenant reads, writes, exports, and nested-object access fail. Run it in CI on every route that accepts an object identifier. 

def test_cannot_read_other_tenant_case(client, tenant_a, tenant_b):
    case_b = make_case(tenant=tenant_b)
    client.force_login(tenant_a.user)
    response = client.get(f"/api/cases/{case_b.public_id}/")
    assert response.status_code in (403, 404)

The assertion should be 403 or 404, not a check on the response body. A serializer that hides a field after the query has already loaded the row is not a tenant boundary; it is a presentation choice.

What good looks like in review

  • Every object query has an explicit tenant scope, and the scope comes from the session.
  • Foreign objects fail closed with 404, not a partial response.
  • Nested resources are scoped through their parent, not through a global lookup.
  • Exports, search, notifications, and background jobs use the same authorization primitive.
  • Two-tenant regression tests run in CI, not as a manual pre-release checklist.
  • Production debug behavior is off, so an exception cannot disclose the query that failed.

None of this is exotic. It is the unglamorous work of putting the boundary where the data is read, instead of hoping every new endpoint remembers a rule. That is the difference between a check and an invariant — and between a test that passes and a tenant boundary that holds.

title: Your WAF only protects the hostname
dek: A web application firewall is a control at one layer. If the origin is still reachable directly, an attacker can choose a different path to the same application — and the WAF never gets a vote.
html:
Most origin-exposure findings are not sophisticated. The organization has a CDN and a WAF. The public hostname resolves to the edge. Everything looks protected. Then a public DNS record, an old staging subdomain, or a certificate transparency entry points to the real hosting address — and a request sent directly there returns the application.

The edge never sees that request. Neither do its bot rules, rate limits, virtual patches, or logging. This is why “we have a WAF” is not an answer to “can the origin be reached directly?”

Where the origin leaks

Origin discovery is an exercise in finding historical and operational trails. Common sources include:

  • SPF and mail records. Hosts authorized to send mail are often the same hosts that serve the application.
  • Certificate transparency. Historical certificates can reveal hostnames and hosting relationships that no longer appear in the current DNS zone.
  • Staging and admin subdomains. Teams protect the production hostname and forget the test environment pointing at the same origin.
  • DNS history and passive data. Previous A records, old providers, and abandoned migrations leave a map.
  • Application behavior. Absolute URLs, redirects, email templates, and error pages sometimes disclose the real host.
  • IPv6. The IPv4 origin is firewalled; the AAAA record is not.
  • Third-party integrations. Partner allowlists, webhooks, and monitoring probes may reveal the origin.

Verifying without becoming the problem

The safe proof is a single direct request to the origin with the public host header, compared against the edge response. In an authorized test, the goal is to show that the origin answers and that edge-only headers or controls are absent. It is not to bypass protections for malicious purposes or to attack a host outside scope. 

# Authorized verification only. Replace placeholders with in-scope values.
curl --resolve <public-host>:443:<origin-address> https://<public-host>/ -I
# Compare:
# - edge response headers (CDN / WAF identifiers)
# - origin response headers
# - behavior of a known edge rule

A successful direct request is not automatically a finding if the origin is intentionally public and protected another way. The finding is that the edge control can be bypassed, which means every protection applied only at the edge is optional from the attacker’s point of view.

Why an IP allowlist alone is not enough

Restricting the origin to the CDN’s published ranges is necessary, but it has two failure modes. First, the list changes and drifts. Second, an allowlist based only on source address can be defeated if the edge does not authenticate the origin connection. The stronger pattern is a network allowlist plus a cryptographic proof that the request came through the edge — authenticated origin pulls, mutual TLS, or a signed header that the origin verifies. 

# Conceptual origin policy
server {
    # Only the edge's egress ranges may connect.
    allow <edge-range-1>;
    allow <edge-range-2>;
    deny  all;
    # Require a verified edge identity (mTLS or signed origin header).
    ssl_client_certificate <edge-ca>;
    ssl_verify_client on;
}

The point is not the exact directive. The point is that the origin should be able to answer “did this request come through the edge?” without trusting the source address alone.

Treat the origin as a private service

If a host does not need to accept traffic from the public internet, it should not. That applies to application origins, admin panels, databases, build agents, and anything that speaks a management protocol.

The management plane is part of the perimeter

Origin exposure often comes with a second problem: management services that were never meant to be public. Remote desktop gateways, database consoles, orchestration dashboards, and staging APIs appear on the same hosting range as the website. Even when they require a login, they expand the credential-attack surface and may carry weaker controls than the production edge.

Move them behind a zero-trust access proxy or VPN, require phishing-resistant MFA and device posture, remove their public DNS records, and alert on new listeners appearing in the range. The goal is not to make the login page prettier; it is to make the service unreachable from the internet.

A practical closure checklist

  • Enumerate every hostname, certificate, and address associated with the estate, including staging and legacy ranges.
  • Verify whether each origin accepts direct requests and whether edge-only controls disappear.
  • Restrict origin ingress to the edge, with authenticated origin pulls or mTLS.
  • Remove public DNS for admin, database, and staging services; place them behind ZTNA.
  • Review SPF, MX, and any other public record that advertises hosting infrastructure.
  • Check IPv6 as carefully as IPv4.
  • Alert on new certificates, hostnames, and listening services outside the approved inventory.
  • Retest from an external network after the change — not from inside the corporate VPN.

A WAF is valuable. It buys time, blocks known patterns, and gives the blue team a control point. But it protects the traffic that reaches it. The origin is a separate security boundary, and it needs to be designed like one.

title: What a rogue VPN service looks like from the inside
dek: A malicious app does not need root to become the device’s network path. It only needs the user to tap “allow” on a VPN consent prompt. Here is what happens next — and what the app can, and cannot, see.
html:
Android’s VpnService is a legitimate API. It lets a user choose an application to route device traffic through a virtual network interface — the basis of corporate VPNs, privacy tools, and traffic analyzers. The permission prompt is the security boundary: the user is handing an app a position of significant control.

In the sample I analysed, the app presented itself as a municipal traffic-notice utility. It did not ask for root. It did not need an exploit. It asked for VPN access, and that was enough to become the device’s egress point.

The manifest is the first signal

Static review starts with capabilities. The interesting permissions were not unusual on their own; the combination was.

  • BIND_VPN_SERVICE — the app can implement a VPN service and receive the user’s consent.
  • RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED — the service can be restarted after a reboot.
  • REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES — the app can prompt the user to install another APK.

A single one of these may be legitimate. Together, they describe an app that can persist, control the network path, and bring in a second stage. That is a dropper pattern, not a traffic-notice app.

The route is the capability

The service built a TUN interface with a private address and a default route. In simplified form, the behavior looks like this: 

VpnService.Builder()
    .addAddress("<tun-address>", 32)
    .addRoute("0.0.0.0", 0)        // default route: all IPv4 egress
    .addDnsServer("<dns-resolver>")
    .establish()

On a real device, the addresses are assigned by the VPN implementation. The important detail is the default route: it pulls traffic from other apps into the VPN process. The app can then forward, inspect, modify, or drop that traffic. That is the same mechanism a legitimate security tool uses — and the same mechanism an attacker can abuse.

The VPN is not a remote server by default. It is a local interface. The malicious app can run a local proxy, forward traffic to its own infrastructure, or simply observe what passes through. The user sees a VPN key in the status bar and may assume they are protected.

The second stage

The initial APK did not contain the full payload. A receiver contacted rotating infrastructure, downloaded an encrypted blob, wrote it to the app’s private cache, decrypted it with a bundled key, and loaded it with DexClassLoader. This keeps the installed package smaller, makes store review harder, and lets the operator change behavior after installation. 

// Behavioral sketch — values and class names removed
download(<encrypted-module>)
  → write(cacheDir/<random>)
  → decrypt(<bundled-key>)
  → DexClassLoader.loadClass(<entry-point>)

Dynamic loading is not inherently malicious — many apps use it for feature modules. In this context, it explained why the visible APK looked incomplete. The real capability arrived after installation.

What it can see — and what it cannot

It is tempting to describe a rogue VPN as “reading every message.” That is usually inaccurate. A local VPN sees the traffic that passes through it, but modern apps use TLS. Without a trusted interception certificate, the VPN sees connection metadata: destinations, DNS queries, SNI in some cases, timing, and volume. Cleartext HTTP is fully visible. TLS content is not.

This does not make the capability harmless. The app can redirect traffic, block updates, inject content into cleartext sessions, profile behavior, and combine the network position with other permissions. It can also prompt the user to install a second payload. The accurate risk is control and follow-on access, not magical decryption.

Precision matters

Overstating what malware can do makes the report easier to dismiss. State the observed capability, the conditions required for more, and the impact that follows. That is more useful to a defender than a dramatic claim.

Detection signals that generalize

Indicators change; behavior is more stable. The following signals are useful across families:

  • An application requesting BIND_VPN_SERVICE that is not an approved VPN or security tool.
  • A VPN route covering all addresses, especially when the app is not a known enterprise VPN.
  • Dynamic DEX loading shortly after installation, particularly from a cache directory.
  • REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES combined with a sideloaded distribution path.
  • DNS queries to unexpected external resolvers, or a sudden change in resolver behavior.
  • Repeated connections to newly registered or rotating domains from a non-browser app.
  • Accessibility or overlay permissions requested alongside network capabilities.

None of these is conclusive alone. Correlate them with installation source, user reports, and network behavior.

Defense: remove the position, not just the sample

Blocking one package is temporary. The durable controls are about who can obtain this position in the first place:

  • Disallow sideloading on managed devices and alert on unknown-source installs.
  • Treat VPN permission as a privileged capability; require approval and log its use.
  • Restrict REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES through MDM policy where possible.
  • Monitor egress for external DNS resolvers, unusual VPN interfaces, and known-bad infrastructure.
  • Pair endpoint detections with a response playbook: remove the app, revoke sessions, rotate credentials, review second-stage activity.

The most important lesson is not about a specific malware family. It is that Android’s permission model gives users the ability to grant away a network position that most people do not understand. Security teams should treat that grant as a control point — and attackers already do.

title: Write findings engineers can actually fix
dek: A penetration test does not reduce risk by producing a document. It reduces risk when someone with commit access understands the finding, agrees on the fix, and ships it. The report exists to make that happen.
html:
I have read a lot of security reports. The weak ones share a shape: a dramatic title, a screenshot, a CVSS score, and a recommendation to “validate input” or “implement proper security.” The finding may be real, but the engineer receiving it has to reverse-engineer the report before they can write a patch.

A useful finding answers five questions quickly: what is wrong, where, why it matters, what exactly to change, and how we will know it is fixed. Everything else is supporting material.

1. Make the title a fact, not a mood

“Critical API vulnerability” is not a title. It tells the reader nothing they can route to a team. A better title names the object and the failure:

Cross-tenant read access on the case-detail endpoint due to missing organization scope

The title should survive being pasted into a ticket with no other context. If it needs the executive summary to make sense, it is not finished.

2. Put impact before methodology

Engineers are busy. Executives are busier. Start with the sentence that explains the consequence: “An authenticated user from one organization can read another organization’s case records by changing the object identifier.” Then add the conditions: authentication required, role required, data exposed, actions possible.

Methodology belongs after impact. The reader should know whether they need to keep reading before they encounter the request dump.

3. Give the smallest reproducible proof

A finding should include the minimum sequence that demonstrates the issue: the request, the relevant state, and the observed result. Remove unrelated headers, tokens, cookies, and client data. Use placeholders consistently. 

# Minimal proof — values sanitized
1. Sign in as Tenant A.
2. Request /api/<resource>/<tenant-b-object>.
3. Observe HTTP 200 with Tenant B's record.
Expected: 403 or 404.

Do not paste a 400-line proxy history. Link to a redacted evidence file if more detail is needed. The report should be readable; the appendix can be exhaustive.

4. Separate the symptom from the root cause

“The endpoint returns another tenant’s record” is the symptom. The root cause might be a global queryset, a missing object permission, a serializer that fetches related objects without scoping, or a background job that bypasses the request layer.

If the root cause is not confirmed, say so. “The likely cause is a global lookup; the exact call path should be confirmed during remediation” is more honest than inventing certainty. Engineers will trust the report more when it distinguishes observation from inference.

Useful distinction

Observation: what the response showed. Inference: why the code probably behaves that way. Recommendation: what to change. Do not blur the three.

5. Recommend a change, not a virtue

“Sanitize input” is not actionable. “Replace the extension blocklist with a canonicalized allowlist, verify magic bytes, and store uploads outside the web root” is. The recommendation should identify the control, the location, and the acceptance criterion.

  • Control: what mechanism should exist.
  • Location: which component or layer should own it.
  • Acceptance: what a retest will observe when it is correct.

Where possible, include a short code sketch. Keep it illustrative, not a full patch. The engineering team owns the implementation; the report owns the security requirement.

6. Make severity explain itself

CVSS is useful for consistency, not for communication. A score without a rationale is noise. Explain the inputs: what access is needed, what data or capability is reached, what user interaction is required, and what compensating controls exist.

If a finding is high impact but difficult to exploit, say both. If it is easy but limited, say that too. The goal is a defensible priority, not a dramatic number.

7. Close the loop with a retest

The report should define what fixed means before the fix is written. That turns the retest into a verification step rather than a negotiation. For the tenant example, fixed means: the original request returns 403/404, the collection endpoint returns only own-tenant rows, the write path rejects the foreign object, and the regression test runs in CI.

A closure memo is short: what was tested, what changed, what passed, what remains. It gives the client evidence for auditors and gives the engineering team a clean end state.

A compact finding template

Title: [Object] + [failure] + [condition]
Impact: one sentence, business language
Affected: component, endpoint, role, environment
Evidence: minimal reproducible sequence
Root cause: confirmed / likely, with code reference
Fix: control + location + acceptance criteria
Severity: rating + rationale
Retest: exact checks that must pass
References: standards, CWE, related findings

This is not a template problem. It is a respect problem. The report is written for the person who has to change the system, not for the person who wants to look thorough. The best finding is the one that gets fixed quietly, correctly, and without a follow-up meeting to explain what it meant.
